answer: Maturation bias occurs when outcomes improve naturally over time and a simple before-and-after comparison credits the program for changes that would have happened anyway. The tutorial follows a screening rate that rose from 42% in 2014 to 52% at a 2019 program launch and 62% by 2024, a steady gain of about 2 points per year both before and after the program. Because the outcome was already climbing at the same pace, continued improvement is not evidence the program worked. Examining pre-program trends, using a comparison group, and extending the baseline guard against this illusion.

faqs.q: What causes outcomes to improve without a program?
faqs.a: Natural trends can come from growing public awareness, broader policy shifts, demographic change, or other forces that move outcomes over time. The tutorial shows screening rates rising about 2 points per year before any program existed.

faqs.q: Why is a before-and-after comparison weak against maturation?
faqs.a: If the outcome was already trending upward, the after value will exceed the before value regardless of the program. The tutorial's rates climbed at the same 2 points per year before and after launch, so the change cannot be credited to the program.

faqs.q: How can an evaluation guard against maturation bias?
faqs.a: The tutorial recommends looking at pre-program trends, using a comparison group that did not receive the program, extending the baseline, and reporting honestly so that a continuing trend is not mistaken for a program effect.
